name: Sovereign by Necessity: The Collapse and the Charter Years
description: Produced by an early independent coalition that would later be absorbed into what became Vantablack's Documentary Division, this meticulously researched holographic documentary traces the seventy-year dissolution of national governments across the North American interior, focusing on the Great Lakes corridor's transformation from contested municipal wreckage into the corponation sovereignty framework codified by the Sable Charter. Drawing on recovered government archives, personal testimony from surviving civic administrators, and reconstructed session recordings from the final Chicago municipal council meetings of 2143, it remains one of the few pre-Vantablack-absorption works that treats corponation sovereignty as a historical outcome rather than an inevitability — a distinction that made it quietly controversial even at release. Its original holographic runtime is six hours and forty minutes; the licensed Vantablack re-release of 2201 runs four hours and twelve minutes.
cultural_impact: For the generation that came of age in the 2190s, this documentary was the primary source of any critical framework for understanding how corponation sovereignty came to exist, and its erasure from the standard licensed version is itself now taught — in underground study circles — as a case study in the history the film was trying to preserve.
story_hooks: A Tier 3 academic contacts the players needing help sourcing an original pre-absorption print of the full six-hour cut — she believes the excised fourth chapter contains specific names that explain a current political situation, and she is being watched.

One of the surviving civic administrators interviewed in the documentary is still alive in 2226, extremely elderly, and has never spoken publicly again — but someone has been leaving copies of the original cut outside her registered address.

Cross-referencing the reconstructed 2143 council session recordings in the documentary against a recently surfaced archive suggests one of the recordings was fabricated — which means either the documentary's makers were deceived, or they were complicit in establishing a false historical record.
